Mayonnaise

Mayonnaise
TypeSauce
Place of originFrance or Spain (disputed)
Serving temperatureCold

Mayonnaise, often shortened to "mayo", is a thick, cold, creamy sauce or dressing eaten on sandwiches, burgers, salads and chips.[1] It is also the base of several other sauces, among them tartar sauce, remoulade and aioli.

Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil, egg yolk and an acid, either vinegar or lemon juice; many versions add mustard or other flavourings. Its colour ranges from nearly white to pale yellow, and its texture from a light cream to a thick gel.[2]

Etymology

The origin of the name is disputed. One account links it to the town of Mahón on Menorca, taken by French forces in 1756; another derives it from an old French word for egg yolk.[3]

History

Sauces of oil and egg were known in Mediterranean cooking long before the name appeared. Early French recipes for the sauce were made with olive oil and beaten by hand with a fork or a whisk, which took a long time.[4] Commercial mayonnaise was first sold in jars in New York in the early twentieth century, and by the 1920s it was made in factories in large quantities.

Preparation

Mayonnaise is made by slowly adding oil to egg yolk while whisking hard, so that the oil is broken into tiny droplets. The lecithin in the yolk is the emulsifier that keeps the droplets apart. If the oil is added too fast the sauce separates; it can usually be rescued by starting again with a fresh yolk and adding the broken sauce to it a little at a time.

A blender or food processor makes the work quicker. Recipes made with a whole egg instead of the yolk give a lighter sauce. A typical home recipe uses about 150 ml of oil for each yolk.

Commercial mayonnaise

Commercial mayonnaise is usually made with soybean or rapeseed oil rather than olive oil, and with pasteurised egg yolk. It may contain up to 80% oil by weight. Reduced-fat versions replace part of the oil with water and starch, and are made with thickeners such as xanthan gum.[5]

Large amounts of mayonnaise are sold in single-serving sachets to restaurants. Because the acid and the salt slow the growth of bacteria, unopened jars keep for months.

Variants

  • Aioli, made with garlic and olive oil, from the Mediterranean coast
  • Vegan mayonnaise is made from aquafaba, the cooking water of chickpeas, or from soy milk, in place of the egg
  • Kewpie, a Japanese brand made with rice vinegar and egg yolks only
  • Remoulade is mayonnaise mixed with herbs, capers and chopped pickles

Food safety

Home-made mayonnaise made with raw egg can carry Salmonella bacteria. Health agencies advise using pasteurised eggs for sauces that will not be cooked, and keeping the sauce cold.[6]

Cement

A cement is a binder, a substance used in construction that sets and hardens and sticks to other materials, binding them together.[1] Cement is seldom used on its own; it is mixed with sand and gravel (aggregate) to make concrete, or with sand alone to make mortar.

The most common cement today is Portland cement, produced by heating limestone with clay or shale to about 1,450 °C in a kiln, and grinding the resulting clinker with a little gypsum.[2] Cements are hydraulic, which set by reacting with water and harden even under water, or non-hydraulic, which set by reacting with carbon dioxide in the air.

History

Ancient times

Lime mortars were used in the ancient Near East and in Egypt. Roman concrete was made from lime and volcanic ash (pozzolana), which reacts with lime and water to give a hard, durable stone; some Roman harbour walls still stand after two thousand years.[3]

Modern cement

In 1824 the English builder Joseph Aspdin patented a cement he called Portland cement, after the stone of the Isle of Portland that it resembled when set. Modern Portland cement, burned at a higher temperature, dates from the 1840s.

Chemistry

Portland cement clinker consists of four main minerals: alite (tricalcium silicate), belite (dicalcium silicate), tricalcium aluminate and a calcium aluminoferrite. When water is added, these minerals form calcium silicate hydrate, the glue that gives concrete its strength.[4]

The composition of the raw mix is controlled closely; small amounts of iron ore or sand may be added to correct it.

Uses

Concrete made with cement is the most widely used building material in the world. Mortar is a mixture of cement, sand and water used to bed bricks and stones. Grout and render are made with cement too.

Environmental impact

Cement manufacture releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, both from burning fuel and from the limestone itself as it is heated. Cement is responsible for about 8% of the world’s carbon dioxide emissions.[5] Blended cements, made with fly ash or slag in place of part of the clinker, release less.

Safety

Wet cement is strongly alkaline and can cause chemical burns to skin and eyes. Gloves, eye protection and long sleeves are advised; skin that has touched wet cement should be washed with clean water.

Glass

Glass is a hard, brittle and usually transparent solid that has no crystal structure.[1] It is used for windows, bottles, tableware and lenses.

Most glass is silicate glass, based on silica (silicon dioxide), the main part of sand. Ordinary window and bottle glass is soda–lime glass, roughly 70% silica, 15% soda (sodium oxide) and 9% lime (calcium oxide), with small amounts of other oxides.[2] The soda lowers the melting point of the silica, and the lime makes the glass resistant to water.

History

Natural glass such as obsidian, formed from volcanic lava, was used to make sharp tools in the Stone Age. Glass making began in Mesopotamia about 3,500 years ago; early beads and vessels were made from sand mixed with plant ash.[3]

Glassblowing, invented in the eastern Mediterranean in the first century BC, made glass cheap enough for everyday use. Medieval glassmakers in the forests of Europe used wood ash as the flux, and their glass was often greenish.

Manufacture

Modern glass is made by melting a mixture of sand, soda ash and limestone in a furnace at about 1,500 °C. Broken glass, called cullet, is added to the batch because it melts more easily and saves energy.[4] Flat glass for windows is made by floating the molten glass on a bath of molten tin.

Types

  • Borosilicate glass, made with boron oxide, expands little when heated and is used for laboratory and oven ware
  • Lead glass (crystal) contains lead oxide, which makes it sparkle
  • Fused quartz is nearly pure silica and withstands very high temperatures
  • Toughened glass is cooled quickly so that its surface is in compression; it breaks into small blunt pieces

Recycling

Glass can be recycled without loss of quality. Bottles are sorted by colour, crushed and remelted. Recycling one tonne of glass saves about 1.2 tonnes of raw materials.

Bread

Bread
TypeStaple food
Main ingredientsFlour, water
VariationsLeavened, unleavened
Food energy (per 100 g serving)265 kcal

Bread is a staple food prepared from a dough of flour and water, usually by baking.[1] Throughout recorded history and around the world it has been an important part of many cultures’ diets.

Bread may be leavened by natural yeasts and bacteria (as in sourdough), by baker’s yeast, by chemical raising agents such as baking soda, or by air beaten into the batter. Unleavened breads are flat.

Etymology

The Old English word bread meant a piece or morsel; the usual word for the food was hlaf, from which "loaf" comes.

History

Bread is one of the oldest prepared foods. Charred crumbs of a flatbread made from wild cereals and the roots of club-rush, about 14,400 years old, were found at a site in Jordan.[2] Leavened bread was baked in ancient Egypt, where bakers kept back a little of each dough to start the next.

Types

Breads are grouped by how they are leavened and how they are cooked.

  • Flatbreads
    • Chapati, an unleavened wheat flatbread of India and East Africa, cooked on a dry griddle called a tawa
    • Injera, a spongy sour flatbread of Ethiopia and Eritrea made from teff flour fermented for several days
    • Tortilla, a thin Mexican flatbread of maize treated with lime (nixtamal) or of wheat
    • Pita, a round pocket bread of the eastern Mediterranean that puffs up in a very hot oven
    • Naan, a leavened flatbread of South and Central Asia baked against the wall of a clay tandoor oven
  • Loaves
    • Sourdough bread, leavened with a culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria kept going by regular feeding
    • Rye bread, dense and dark, common in Germany, Scandinavia and Eastern Europe
    • Soda bread, an Irish quick bread raised with baking soda and buttermilk instead of yeast
  • Steamed breads
    • Mantou, a soft white steamed bun of northern China, eaten plain or with savoury dishes

Ingredients

Flour

Flour supplies the starch and the proteins that form gluten. Wheat flour is preferred for raised bread because its gluten traps the gas made by the yeast; rye and barley flours make denser loaves.[3]

Liquids

Water is the usual liquid. A typical dough is about 60 to 65 parts water to 100 parts flour by weight; milk, beer or whey may be used in its place.

Leavening

Yeast

Baker’s yeast ferments the sugars in the dough to carbon dioxide and alcohol. The gas raises the dough; the alcohol evaporates in the oven.

Chemical leavening

Baking soda reacts with an acid such as buttermilk to release carbon dioxide at once, so soda breads go straight into the oven.

Salt

Salt, about 2% of the flour weight, strengthens the gluten and slows the yeast, and gives flavour.

Nutrition

White bread is mostly carbohydrate, with about 9% protein and little fat. Wholemeal bread keeps the bran and germ and has more fibre, iron and B vitamins. In many countries white flour is fortified with iron, calcium and folic acid by law.[4]

Notes

  • Weights in recipes in this article are given for flour at 14% moisture, the usual commercial standard
  • A loaf baked in a tin is called a tin loaf; a free-standing loaf is a cob or a boule

Timeline of antibiotics

This is a timeline of the discovery and introduction of antibiotics, the medicines that kill bacteria or stop them growing.[1] Dates are those of discovery or first report; the year a drug came into general use is often several years later.

Before 1940

  • 1909
    • Paul Ehrlich and Sahachiro Hata find arsphenamine (Salvarsan), an arsenic compound active against syphilis, the first modern antimicrobial drug
  • 1928
    • Alexander Fleming notices that a mould, Penicillium notatum, has killed the bacteria around it on a culture plate in his London laboratory
    • Fleming names the active substance penicillin but cannot purify it in useful amounts
  • 1932
    • Gerhard Domagk at Bayer finds that the red dye Prontosil cures streptococcal infections in mice, the first sulfonamide
  • 1939
    • René Dubos isolates gramicidin from a soil bacterium, the first antibiotic made commercially

1940–1960

  • 1940
    • Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley at Oxford purify penicillin and show that it protects infected mice
  • 1943
    • Albert Schatz and Selman Waksman discover streptomycin in a soil organism, the first drug that works against tuberculosis
    • Mass production of penicillin in deep fermentation tanks begins in the United States
  • 1948
    • Benjamin Duggar describes chlortetracycline, the first tetracycline, from a soil sample taken in Missouri
  • 1952
    • Erythromycin is isolated from a soil bacterium collected in the Philippines

After 1960

  • 1961
    • Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is first reported in Britain, two years after methicillin came into use
  • 1987
    • The last new class of antibiotics for nearly three decades (the lipopeptides) is discovered
  • 2015
    • Teixobactin is reported, found by growing soil bacteria in a device placed back in the soil

pages.wikipedia/Glossary_of_carpentry:
Glossary of carpentry

This glossary of carpentry lists terms used in carpentry, joinery and timber framing.[1]

A–D

Arris
The sharp edge where two flat surfaces of a piece of wood meet. Arrises are often eased with a plane or sandpaper so that they do not splinter.
Batten
A thin strip of wood used to hold panels in place, to fix roof tiles to, or as a temporary straight edge.
Biscuit joint
A joint in which an oval wafer of compressed beech is glued into matching slots cut in both pieces with a biscuit jointer.
Dado
A groove cut across the grain of a board, into which another board fits; called a housing in Britain.
Dovetail
A joint of interlocking wedge-shaped tails and pins, very strong in tension; used for drawers and boxes.

E–M

Kerf
The width of the cut made by a saw blade. A thin-kerf blade wastes less wood but bends more easily.
Mortise and tenon
A joint in which a projecting tongue (the tenon) on one piece fits a hole (the mortise) in the other, often pinned with a wooden peg.
Mitre
A joint in which the two pieces are cut at an angle, usually 45 degrees each, to make a corner.

N–Z

Rebate
A step-shaped recess cut along the edge of a board; called a rabbet in North America.
Sapwood
The younger, outer wood of a tree, lighter in colour and less resistant to rot than the heartwood.
Tongue and groove
Boards with a ridge on one edge and a groove on the other, so that they fit together side by side to make a floor or a wall.

Mombasa

Mombasa
CountryKenya
CountyMombasa County
Population (2019)1,208,333
Elevation50 m
Time zoneUTC+3 (EAT)

Mombasa is a coastal city in south-eastern Kenya, on the Indian Ocean. It is the country’s oldest and second-largest city, with a population of about 1.2 million at the 2019 census.[1]

The city centre stands on Mombasa Island, joined to the mainland by bridges, a causeway and a ferry. Its port, Kilindini Harbour, is the largest in East Africa and serves Uganda, Rwanda and South Sudan as well as Kenya.

History

Mombasa was a Swahili trading town by the twelfth century. The Portuguese built Fort Jesus there in 1593–1596; the fort later passed to the Omani Arabs and then to the British. It is now a museum and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.[2]

Geography

Climate

Mombasa has a tropical wet and dry climate. The long rains fall from April to June and the short rains in October and November; the average high temperature is 30 °C in February and 27 °C in July.

Transport

Arrival by air

Moi International Airport, 10 km west of the city centre, has flights to Nairobi and to several cities in Europe and the Middle East.

Rail

The Madaraka Express standard-gauge railway, opened in 2017, links Mombasa with Nairobi in about five hours. The terminus is at Miritini, on the mainland, about 15 km from the island.[3]

Ferry

The Likoni Ferry carries pedestrians and vehicles across the harbour mouth to the south coast. It runs day and night and is free for people on foot.

Economy

The port, tourism and light industry are the main employers. The city has a large oil refinery and a free-trade zone.

Culture

See

Visitors come to see the Old Town, with its narrow streets, carved wooden doors and balconies, the best known part of the city.

Notes

Population figures are for Mombasa County, which is the same area as the city. Earlier censuses counted a smaller area.

Sources

Much of the history in this article is drawn from the Pate and Mombasa chronicles, Swahili histories written down in the nineteenth century.

pages.wikipedia/Water_purification:
Water purification

Water purification is the process of removing chemicals, biological contaminants, suspended solids and gases from water, to make it fit for drinking or for another purpose.[1]

Methods include physical processes such as filtration and sedimentation, biological processes such as slow sand filters, chemical processes such as chlorination, and the use of radiation such as ultraviolet light.

Methods for households

Where piped water is not safe, water can be treated at home. The World Health Organization lists several methods that remove or kill most germs.[2]

  • Boiling
    • Bring the water to a rolling boil for one minute; at altitudes above 2,000 metres, boil for three minutes because water boils at a lower temperature there
    • Let it cool in the covered pot and store it in a clean container with a lid
  • Chlorination
    • Add household bleach of 5–6% sodium hypochlorite, two drops per litre of clear water, or four drops per litre if the water is cloudy or very cold
    • Stir and wait at least 30 minutes before drinking; the water should have a slight smell of chlorine
  • Solar disinfection
    • Fill clear plastic PET bottles of up to 2 litres with clear water and lay them in full sun for six hours, or for two days if the sky is more than half cloudy
  • Filtration
    • Ceramic filters with very fine pores remove bacteria and protozoa but not all viruses, and must be cleaned regularly
    • A cloth folded several times removes larger particles and some cholera bacteria attached to plankton

Municipal treatment

  1. Coagulation and flocculation: chemicals such as aluminium sulfate are added, which make fine particles clump together
  2. Sedimentation: the clumps settle to the bottom of large tanks
  3. Filtration: the clear water passes through beds of sand and gravel, and sometimes activated carbon
  4. Disinfection: chlorine, chloramine, ozone or ultraviolet light kills remaining germs; a small residue of chlorine is left in the pipes

History

The first municipal sand filters were built at Paisley, Scotland, in 1804. Chlorination of public water began in Jersey City in 1908, and typhoid deaths fell sharply in the cities that adopted it.[3]

pages.wikipedia/Soap:
Soap

Soap is a salt of a fatty acid used for washing, bathing and cleaning.[1] In a household setting, "soap" usually means a bar or liquid made for washing the body.

Soaps are mainly produced by treating vegetable or animal oils and fats with a strong base, such as sodium hydroxide (lye) for hard soap or potassium hydroxide for soft soap. This reaction is called saponification.

History

The earliest recorded soap is described on Babylonian clay tablets of about 2800 BC, which give a recipe of fats boiled with ashes. The Romans made soap from tallow and the ash of beech wood. Aleppo soap, made with olive oil and laurel oil, has been made in Syria for over a thousand years.[2]

Making soap

Cold process

In the cold process the fats are mixed with a lye solution at about 40 °C and poured into moulds. The soap must cure for four to six weeks before use, so that saponification finishes and the bar hardens.

The amount of lye is worked out from the saponification value of each oil. Recipes usually use slightly less lye than is needed to react with all the fat, so that no free lye is left in the bar.

Hot process

In the hot process the mixture is cooked until saponification is complete, so the soap can be used sooner.

How soap cleans

Each soap molecule has a tail that mixes with oil and a head that mixes with water. In water, the molecules surround droplets of grease in tiny balls called micelles, which are rinsed away. Washing hands with soap and water for 20 seconds removes most germs.[3]

Safety

Lye is very caustic. It should be added to water, never water to lye, while wearing gloves and eye protection, and kept away from children.

Jupiter

Jupiter
Mean radius69,911 km
Mass1.8982×10^27 kg
Orbital period11.86 years
Surface gravity24.79 m/s^2
Composition by volume89% hydrogen, 10% helium

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the Solar System. It is a gas giant with a mass more than two and a half times that of all the other planets combined.[1]

Jupiter is the third-brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon and Venus, and has been known since ancient times. It is named after the chief god of Roman mythology.

Physical characteristics

Composition

Jupiter’s upper atmosphere is about 90% hydrogen and 10% helium by number of molecules. By mass, the planet is roughly 71% hydrogen, 24% helium and 5% heavier elements.[2] The atmosphere holds traces of methane, water vapour, ammonia and silicon compounds.

Size and mass

Jupiter’s equatorial diameter is 142,984 km, eleven times that of Earth. Its mass is 318 times Earth’s. It spins faster than any other planet, once every 9 hours 56 minutes, which flattens it at the poles.

Internal structure

Below the cloud tops, hydrogen is squeezed into a liquid, and deeper still into metallic hydrogen, which conducts electricity and produces the planet’s strong magnetic field. Measurements by the Juno spacecraft suggest a large, diffuse core of rock and ice mixed with hydrogen.[3]

Moons

Jupiter has at least 95 known moons. The four largest, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, were discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610. Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury.

Exploration

Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter, in 1973. Galileo orbited the planet from 1995 to 2003, and Juno has orbited it since 2016.

pages.wikipedia/Gunpowder:
Gunpowder

Gunpowder, also called black powder, is the earliest known chemical explosive.[1] It was invented in China during the Tang dynasty, in the ninth century.

It is a mixture of sulfur, charcoal and potassium nitrate (saltpetre). The sulfur and charcoal act as fuels while the saltpetre is an oxidiser.

History

Chinese alchemists searching for an elixir of life found that saltpetre, sulfur and charcoal burned violently together. By the eleventh century gunpowder was used in fire arrows and bombs, and by the thirteenth in guns.[2]

Composition

The standard modern proportions are 75% potassium nitrate, 15% charcoal and 10% sulfur by weight. Early Chinese and European mixtures held less saltpetre and burned more slowly.

The size of the grains controls how fast the powder burns: fine powder burns quickly and was used for priming, coarse powder for large cannon.

Uses

Gunpowder was replaced in firearms by smokeless powders from the 1880s. It is still used in fireworks, in some blasting and in muzzle-loading guns.

Safety

Black powder is sensitive to sparks, friction and static electricity, and should be stored only in small amounts in approved containers.

pages.wikimed/Choking:
Choking

Choking is when a foreign object or food blocks the airway, stopping a person from breathing.[1] A complete blockage is an emergency: without help, the person can lose consciousness within minutes.

Signs of choking include clutching the throat, being unable to speak, cry or cough, noisy or no breathing, and skin turning blue or grey.

Causes

In adults, choking is most often on food, especially meat, while eating quickly, talking or after drinking alcohol. Young children choke on small toys, coins, nuts, grapes and hard sweets.

First aid

If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing and do not hit their back. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe:[2]

  1. Give up to five back blows
    • Stand behind and slightly to one side, support the chest with one hand and lean the person well forward
    • Strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand, checking after each blow whether the blockage has cleared
  2. If back blows fail, give up to five abdominal thrusts
    • Stand behind the person, put your arms around the upper abdomen and make a fist just above the navel
    • Grasp the fist with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards
  3. Call emergency services if the blockage has not cleared, and keep alternating five back blows with five abdominal thrusts
  4. If the person becomes unconscious, lower them to the ground, call for help and start cardiopulmonary resuscitation with chest compressions

Infants

For a baby under one year, abdominal thrusts are not used. Lay the baby face down along your forearm, head lower than the body, and give up to five back blows; then turn the baby face up and give up to five chest thrusts with two fingers in the middle of the chest.

Pregnant or obese people

If you cannot get your arms around the abdomen, give chest thrusts instead, with your fist on the lower half of the breastbone.

After care

Anyone who has been given abdominal thrusts should be seen by a doctor afterwards, as the thrusts can cause internal injury.

Prevention

  • Cut food for young children into small pieces, and cut grapes lengthwise into quarters
  • Keep coins, button batteries and small toy parts out of the reach of children under three

pages.wikimed/Heat_stroke:
Heat stroke

Heat stroke is a severe heat illness that results in a body temperature greater than 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), along with red skin, headache, dizziness and confusion.[1] Sweating is generally present in exertional heat stroke but not in classic heat stroke.

It is a medical emergency; without prompt treatment it can damage the brain, kidneys and muscles and can kill.

Signs and symptoms

  • High body temperature, measured in the rectum if possible
  • Confusion, slurred speech, agitation, seizures or loss of consciousness
  • Hot, red skin, which may be dry or wet
  • Fast breathing and a racing pulse

Causes

Classic heat stroke affects older people, young children and the chronically ill during heat waves. Exertional heat stroke affects healthy people, such as soldiers, labourers and athletes, who work hard in hot weather.

Treatment

Treatment is rapid cooling while emergency help is on its way. The aim is to bring the body temperature down to about 39 °C as quickly as possible.[2]

  • Cooling methods
    • Immersion of the body up to the neck in cold or iced water is the fastest method for exertional heat stroke and is used by sports and military medical teams
    • Where immersion is not possible, spray or sponge the skin with cool water and fan it, and put ice packs in the armpits, groin and on the neck
  • Move the person to a cool, shaded place and remove extra clothing
  • Do not give paracetamol or aspirin: they do not lower a temperature caused by heat stroke
  • Give sips of cool water only if the person is fully awake and able to swallow

Prevention

Drink plenty of water in hot weather, avoid hard work in the hottest part of the day, wear light loose clothing, and check on elderly neighbours during heat waves.

pages.wikipedia/Brass:
Brass

Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, in proportions which can be varied to achieve different colours and mechanical, electrical, acoustic and chemical properties.[1]

Brass is similar to bronze, another copper alloy that uses tin instead of zinc. It has a bright gold-like appearance and is used for decoration, for locks, gears, valves and plumbing fittings, and for musical instruments.

Types

  • Cartridge brass, 70% copper and 30% zinc, is easy to shape cold and is used for ammunition cases
  • Naval brass adds about 1% tin to resist corrosion in sea water
  • Leaded brass, with up to 3% lead, is easy to machine but is no longer used for drinking-water fittings in many countries

History

Early brass was made by the cementation process, in which copper and zinc ore were heated together until zinc vapour was absorbed by the copper. The Romans made brass coins this way.

Recycling

Around 90% of brass alloys are recycled. Because brass is not magnetic, it can be separated from iron scrap with a strong magnet.

pages.wikipedia/Compost:
Compost

Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil, made by decomposing plant and food waste and recycling organic materials.[1]

A good compost heap needs a balance of nitrogen-rich "green" material and carbon-rich "brown" material, enough water to be as damp as a wrung-out sponge, and air.

Materials

  • Greens (rich in nitrogen)
    • Vegetable and fruit peelings, coffee grounds and tea leaves
    • Fresh grass clippings, added in thin layers so they do not mat together
    • Manure from cows, horses, chickens or rabbits
  • Browns (rich in carbon)
    • Dry leaves, straw and sawdust
    • Shredded paper and cardboard, without glossy coatings
  • What not to add
    • Meat, fish, dairy and cooked food, which attract rats and flies
    • Dog and cat faeces, which can carry parasites
    • Diseased plants and the roots of perennial weeds

Ratio

The ideal ratio of carbon to nitrogen is about 25 to 30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen. In practice gardeners use roughly two to three buckets of browns for every bucket of greens.

Process

Bacteria and fungi break down the material. A large heap heats up to 55–70 °C in its centre within a few days, which kills most weed seeds and disease organisms. The heap should be turned every week or two to let air in; finished compost is dark, crumbly and smells of earth, and takes two to six months.[2]

Uses

Compost is dug into soil or spread on top as a mulch. It improves the structure of clay and sandy soils, holds water, and feeds soil life.

pages.wikipedia/Stainless_steel:
Stainless steel

Stainless steel is an alloy of iron that is resistant to rusting and corrosion.[1] It contains at least 10.5% chromium and usually nickel, and may also contain other elements, such as molybdenum, carbon and nitrogen.

The chromium forms a thin film of chromium oxide on the surface, invisible to the eye, which protects the metal underneath and heals itself if scratched.

History

Harry Brearley of Sheffield is often credited with the first true stainless steel in 1913, made while looking for a metal for gun barrels that would not wear. Sheffield cutlers were soon making knives from it.[2]

Grades

  • Type 304, the most common grade, contains 18% chromium and 8% nickel and is used for sinks, cookware and food equipment
  • Type 316 adds 2–3% molybdenum, which resists salt water and chlorides, and is used for boat fittings and surgical instruments
  • Type 430 has no nickel; it is magnetic and cheaper, and is used for appliance panels

Production

Stainless steel is made from scrap and ferrochromium melted in an electric arc furnace. Large amounts of nickel are mined in Indonesia and the Philippines for the industry. Around 58 million tonnes were made in 2021.

Corrosion

Stainless steel can still corrode in salt water, in stagnant water or where the oxide film is starved of oxygen, for example under a gasket. This is called crevice corrosion.

pages.wikivoyage/Mombasa:
Mombasa

Mombasa

Mombasa is Kenya’s second city and its main port, an old Swahili trading town on an island in the Indian Ocean. Most visitors pass through on the way to the beaches north and south of the city, but the Old Town and Fort Jesus are worth a day or two.

Understand

History

Arab, Persian and Indian traders were calling at Mombasa a thousand years ago. The Portuguese arrived in 1498 and built Fort Jesus a century later; the Omanis took the town in 1698 and held it, on and off, until the British came in the nineteenth century.

Climate

It is hot and humid all year, with highs around 30°C. The long rains come from April to June and the short rains in November. The most comfortable months are July to September, when the monsoon wind blows from the south.

Tourist information

The Mombasa and Coast Tourist Office on Moi Avenue, near the giant aluminium tusks, has maps and lists of licensed guides.

Get in

By plane

  • Moi International Airport (MBA), Port Reitz, 10 km west of the island, ☎ +254 20 3577058. Flights from Nairobi take an hour and leave many times a day; there are also direct flights from Addis Ababa, Doha, Istanbul and several European cities in the winter season.

From the airport, a taxi to the city centre costs about KSh 1,500 and takes 30 minutes, more in the evening rush. Matatus run from the main road outside the airport gate to the centre for KSh 50, but are crowded and awkward with luggage.

By train

The Madaraka Express runs twice a day between Nairobi and Mombasa on the standard-gauge railway and takes about six hours. Tickets must be bought in advance with M-Pesa or at the station, and passports or Kenyan ID are checked at the entrance.

The Mombasa terminus is at Miritini on the mainland, 15 km from the island. A shuttle bus meets each train and goes to the city centre for KSh 100; taxis wait outside too.

By bus

Many companies run buses to Nairobi, day and night, taking eight to ten hours. Buses leave from offices along Jomo Kenyatta Avenue and Abdel Nasser Road. Night buses are cheaper but accidents are more common at night.

By boat

There is no regular passenger ship to Zanzibar or Dar es Salaam. Dhows sail along the coast, but they are not licensed to carry tourists and are not safe in rough weather.

Get around

The island is small and the Old Town is best seen on foot. For longer trips there are matatus, tuk-tuks, motorbike taxis and ordinary taxis; Uber and Bolt both work in the city.

Traffic over the Nyali Bridge to the north coast can be very slow in the morning and evening.

By matatu

Matatus are minibuses that run fixed routes for a fixed fare, usually KSh 30–80. The main stage for the north coast is on Abdel Nasser Road, and for Likoni on Digo Road. Ask the conductor where to get off.

By tuk-tuk

Three-wheeled tuk-tuks are everywhere on the island and cost KSh 100–300 for a short trip. Agree the fare before you get in, or use the Bolt app, which also books tuk-tuks.

By boda-boda

Motorbike taxis, called boda-bodas, are the quickest way through traffic but have a poor safety record. Insist on a helmet.

By ferry

The Likoni Ferry crosses to the south coast every few minutes, day and night. It is free for foot passengers; cars pay a small toll. It is very crowded at rush hour, and pickpockets work the queue.

By bicycle

Bicycles can be hired from a shop near Fort Jesus for about KSh 800 a day, but the heat and traffic make cycling hard work outside the Old Town.

See

  • Fort Jesus, Nkrumah Road. Daily 08:00–18:00. Adults KSh 1,200 for foreigners. The Portuguese fort, now a museum, with a small collection of finds from a sunken frigate. Guides at the gate charge about KSh 500.
  • Old Town. Narrow lanes of carved doors and balconies between Fort Jesus and the old harbour. Go in the morning, when it is cooler, and dress modestly: it is a Muslim neighbourhood.
  • Haller Park, Bamburi, 10 km north of the city. Daily 08:00–17:00. A former limestone quarry turned into a nature park, with giraffes, hippos and giant tortoises. Feeding time for the giraffes is at 15:00.
  • The Tusks, Moi Avenue. Two pairs of crossed aluminium tusks over the road, built for a royal visit in 1952.

Do

The beaches are the main reason to come. Nyali, Bamburi and Shanzu are on the north coast, Diani on the south coast an hour away by the ferry and road.

  • Dhow sunset cruise, Old Harbour. From about US$60 including dinner. Sail around the island in a traditional wooden dhow.
  • Snorkelling at Mombasa Marine Park, Nyali. Park fee US$17. Glass-bottom boats go out to the reef from the beach hotels at low tide.

Swimming is safe inside the reef at most beaches, but watch for sea urchins at low tide and do not swim alone after dark.

Buy

Biashara Street is the place for kikoi and kanga cloths. Haggle in the markets; shops with marked prices are fixed. ATMs are common on Moi Avenue and Digo Road, and M-Pesa is accepted almost everywhere.

Tipping is not expected in local restaurants; in tourist restaurants 10% is usual if service is not included.

Eat

Mombasa is the place to try Swahili food: biryani, pilau, fish in coconut sauce, mahamri (sweet fried bread) and bhajia. Street food is cheap and good, and chips mayai (an omelette with chips) is sold everywhere.

Budget

  • Jahazi Coffee House, Ndia Kuu, Old Town. KSh 300–600. Swahili breakfasts and spiced coffee in a restored house.
  • Island Dishes, Kibokoni Road. KSh 400. Popular with locals for biryani and fresh juice.

Mid-range

  • Tamarind Dhow, Nyali. KSh 3,000. Seafood dinners on a dhow.

Drink

Most nightlife is on the north coast, in the bars and clubs of Nyali and Bamburi. In the Old Town alcohol is hard to find. Bars usually stay open until about 02:00, and clubs later at weekends.

Sleep

Most visitors stay at the beach hotels on the north or south coast. The few hotels on the island are aimed at business travellers.

Budget

  • New Palm Tree Hotel, Nkrumah Road. Double KSh 3,500. Simple rooms around a courtyard, ten minutes’ walk from Fort Jesus.
  • Mombasa Backpackers, Nyali. Dorm bed KSh 1,500. Pool, kitchen and garden, near the beach.

Mid-range

  • Royal Court Hotel, Haile Selassie Road. Double KSh 9,000. Rooftop restaurant with views over the city.

Near the airport

If you have an early flight, the Port Reitz Airport Inn, two minutes from the terminal, has a free shuttle and rooms from KSh 6,000.

Stay safe

Mombasa is generally safe in the daytime, but muggings happen after dark, especially on the Likoni side and on empty beaches. Take a taxi at night rather than walking.

Beach boys selling tours and souvenirs can be persistent; a firm "no, thank you" usually works. Keep phones out of sight in crowds and on the ferry.

Do not buy drugs: penalties are severe, and some sellers work with the police.

Stay healthy

Malaria is present all year on the coast. Use repellent and a mosquito net, and take antimalarial tablets as advised by a doctor before you travel.

Do not drink tap water; bottled water is sold everywhere. The Aga Khan Hospital on Vanga Road and the Mombasa Hospital on Mama Ngina Drive have 24-hour emergency departments.

Connect

Safaricom and Airtel SIM cards are sold at the airport and in the city; you need your passport to register one.

Go next

  • Diani Beach — white sand an hour to the south
  • Malindi and Watamu — Italian-flavoured resort towns to the north
  • Tsavo East National Park — red elephants, two hours inland
pages.wikivoyage/Mount_Kenya_National_Park:
Mount Kenya National Park

Mount Kenya National Park

Mount Kenya National Park protects the slopes and peaks of Mount Kenya, at 5,199 m the second highest mountain in Africa. Trekkers come for Point Lenana (4,985 m), the highest point that can be reached without technical climbing.

Understand

The mountain is an old volcano on the equator. Its forests, bamboo zone and moorland of giant groundsels are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The two main summits, Batian and Nelion, need rock-climbing skills.

Flora and fauna

Elephants, buffalo and colobus monkeys live in the forest. Rock hyraxes are common near the huts and will steal food. Leopards are present but rarely seen.

Climate

The driest months are January to February and July to September. Nights above 4,000 m are below freezing all year, and afternoon cloud and rain are common.

Get in

The park has several gates. Most treks use one of three routes: the Sirimon route from the north-west, the Naro Moru route from the west and the Chogoria route from the east.

Naro Moru town is three hours from Nairobi by matatu or car on the Nanyuki road. From the town, the park gate is 17 km up a dirt road; a 4WD vehicle is needed in the rainy season. Chogoria gate is reached from Chogoria town by a rough 30-km track.

Fees and permits

Park fees are paid at the gate by card or M-Pesa; cash is not accepted. Foreign adults pay US$52 a day. Every trekker must be accompanied by a registered guide, and guides are hired in Naro Moru, Nanyuki or Chogoria.

Get around

Inside the park, travel is on foot. Porters carry up to 18 kg each and can be hired with the guide.

See

Lake Michaelson, in the Gorges Valley on the Chogoria route, is a deep green lake under cliffs. The Vertical Bog on the Naro Moru route is a steep, wet climb through tussock grass.

Do

Trekking to Point Lenana

Allow four to five days for the climb and descent. A common plan is up the Sirimon route and down Chogoria, which shows both sides of the mountain.

The final climb to Point Lenana starts at about 02:30 from Shipton’s Camp or Austrian Hut, so that trekkers reach the top for sunrise, before the cloud comes up.

Climbing

Batian and Nelion are graded rock climbs; climbers need their own ropes and experience on rock at altitude. The best climbing seasons match the dry months.

Eat

Bring all your food. Cooks can be hired with the guide and will prepare meals at the camps. There is nothing to buy above the gates.

Drink

Water from the streams on the upper mountain is generally clean but should still be boiled or treated, as people and animals use the catchment.

Sleep

There are bunkhouses at Old Moses (3,300 m) and Shipton’s Camp (4,200 m) on the Sirimon route, Met Station and Mackinder’s Camp on Naro Moru, and campsites everywhere. Bunks must be booked in advance in the high season.

Stay safe

Altitude sickness is the main danger. Ascend slowly, spending a night at around 3,300 m before going higher, drink plenty, and go down at once if you have a severe headache, confusion or breathlessness at rest.

Hypothermia is possible even on the equator: bring a warm sleeping bag, a waterproof jacket, a hat and gloves. Do not walk alone, and keep to the trails in the forest because of buffalo.

Go next

  • Nanyuki — a market town on the equator with supplies and hotels
  • Ol Pejeta Conservancy — rhinos and chimpanzees, an hour away
pages.wikivoyage/Lamu:
Lamu

Lamu

Lamu is an island town on the north coast of Kenya, the oldest continuously inhabited Swahili town in East Africa and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. There are almost no cars: people get about on foot, by donkey and by boat.

Understand

Lamu Old Town has narrow lanes of coral-stone houses with carved wooden doors. The population is mostly Muslim and the pace is slow. Shela, a village 3 km along the shore, has the best beach and most of the upmarket hotels.

The Maulidi festival, celebrating the Prophet’s birthday, brings pilgrims from all over East Africa; book rooms early if you visit then.

Get in

By plane

Lamu airport is on Manda Island, across the channel. Several small airlines fly from Nairobi and Mombasa. A boat from the airport jetty to Lamu town takes 10 minutes and costs KSh 200 by the public ferry.

By bus

Buses from Mombasa to Mokowe on the mainland take about seven hours, via Malindi. From Mokowe jetty, ferries cross to Lamu town in 20 minutes. The road has had security problems in the past; check current advice before travelling.

Get around

Walk. The old town is small, and the lanes are too narrow for vehicles.

By donkey

Donkeys carry goods around town, and visitors can ride them along the waterfront. The Donkey Sanctuary on the seafront treats sick and injured donkeys free of charge.

By boat

Motor boats and dhows serve as water taxis between Lamu, Shela and Manda. A boat to Shela costs about KSh 300 per person on a shared boat, or KSh 1,000 for a private one. The walk to Shela along the shore takes 40 minutes.

See

  • Lamu Museum, Waterfront. Daily 08:00–18:00. KSh 500. Swahili culture, the famous carved horn called the siwa, and a reconstructed Swahili house.
  • Lamu Fort, Main Square. Built by the Sultan of Pate in the early nineteenth century; later a prison.

Do

Take a dhow trip to the mangroves, or snorkel near Manda Toto island. Shela Beach stretches for 12 km and is almost empty outside the village.

Eat

Seafood is excellent and cheap: grilled fish, crab and lobster in coconut sauce. Most restaurants close during the day in Ramadan.

Drink

Alcohol is served in only a few hotels; Peponi Hotel in Shela has the best-known bar.

Sleep

Guesthouses in old Swahili houses in town are good value. Shela has more expensive hotels on the beach.

Stay safe

Lamu town itself is safe and friendly. Dress modestly away from the beach. Some governments advise against travel on the mainland road between Malindi and Mokowe; flying in avoids it.

Go next

  • Malindi — by air or a long road trip
  • Kiwayu — a remote island further north, by boat
pages.wikivoyage/Tanzania:
Tanzania

Tanzania

Tanzania is the largest country in East Africa, home to Mount Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti and the islands of Zanzibar.

Regions

  • Northern circuit — Arusha, Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti and Ngorongoro Crater
  • Coast — Dar es Salaam, Bagamoyo and the Swahili towns
  • Zanzibar — the spice islands, semi-autonomous

Understand

Tanzania was formed in 1964 by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar. Swahili is the national language and is spoken almost everywhere; English is used in business and higher education.

Get in

Entry requirements

Most visitors need a visa, which can be obtained online in advance as an e-visa or, for many nationalities, on arrival at the main airports and border posts for US$50 (US$100 for citizens of the United States).

A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if you arrive from, or have spent more than 12 hours in transit in, a country with a risk of yellow fever, which includes Kenya.

By plane

The main international airports are Julius Nyerere International in Dar es Salaam, Kilimanjaro International between Arusha and Moshi, and Zanzibar’s Abeid Amani Karume airport.

By land

The busiest border crossing from Kenya is at Namanga, between Nairobi and Arusha; shuttle buses make the trip in about six hours.

Get around

Buses connect all the main towns and are cheap, but drive fast. The train from Dar es Salaam to Morogoro and Dodoma on the new standard-gauge line is quicker and more comfortable. Domestic flights save long days on the road to the parks.

Ferries run several times a day between Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar, taking about two hours. Buy tickets only at the ferry company offices inside the port gate, and ignore touts.

See

The great wildebeest migration crosses the Serengeti and the Masai Mara between July and October. Ngorongoro Crater is one of the best places in Africa to see black rhino.

Do

Climbing Kilimanjaro takes five to eight days; longer routes give more time to get used to the altitude and a better chance of reaching the top.

Buy

The currency is the Tanzanian shilling. US dollars are widely accepted for park fees and safaris, but notes printed before 2009 are often refused.

Tipping is customary on safari and Kilimanjaro climbs: guides, cooks and porters expect it, and parks publish suggested amounts. In restaurants, rounding up the bill or leaving 10% is appreciated.

Eat

Ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is the staple, eaten with stews of beans, meat or greens. Nyama choma (grilled meat) and chipsi mayai are found everywhere.

Drink

Local beers include Safari, Kilimanjaro and Serengeti. Konyagi is a local spirit.

Sleep

Hotels range from basic guesthouses (gesti) to luxury safari lodges. Prices in the national parks are high because of park concession fees.

Stay safe

Tanzania is generally safe for visitors, but bag snatching and muggings happen in Dar es Salaam and Arusha, especially at night and on beaches. Use registered taxis after dark.

Homosexual acts are illegal and can be punished with long prison terms.

Stay healthy

Malaria is a risk in most of the country below 1,800 m, including Zanzibar. Take antimalarials and use a mosquito net. Tap water is not safe to drink.

Respect

Greetings matter: always greet someone before asking a question. Dress modestly on the coast and in Zanzibar, covering shoulders and knees away from the beach.

Connect

Vodacom, Airtel and Tigo sell SIM cards; registration needs a passport and a fingerprint scan.
pages.wikivoyage/Kungsleden:
Kungsleden

Kungsleden

Kungsleden ("The King’s Trail") is a hiking trail of about 440 km in northern Sweden, between Abisko in the north and Hemavan in the south. The northern section, from Abisko to Kebnekaise, is the most popular.

Understand

The trail crosses mountains, birch forest and open tundra above the Arctic Circle. The Swedish Tourist Association (STF) runs a chain of mountain huts along it, about a day’s walk apart.

Prepare

The hiking season is from late June to late September. Snow can remain on the higher passes until July, and mosquitoes are worst in July. Good waterproof boots and clothing are essential.

Get in

Abisko Turiststation has its own railway station on the line from Kiruna to Narvik; the train from Stockholm takes about 17 hours overnight. Hemavan is reached by bus from Umeå.

Get around

The trail is marked with cairns and red-painted rocks. Large rivers are crossed by bridges; at a few lakes there are rowing boats, and you must leave a boat on each side, which can mean rowing the lake three times.

Go

Abisko to Alesjávri

22 km. The trail follows the Abiskojokk river through birch forest and climbs gently above the tree line.

Alesjávri to Kebnekaise

About 70 km in four days, over the Tjäktja pass (1,140 m), the highest point on the northern section.

Sleep

STF huts have bunks, a kitchen and a wood stove; most have a small shop. Members pay less. Camping is allowed anywhere under the right of public access, but not right next to the huts.

Eat

The hut shops sell dried food, pasta and chocolate, but prices are high and choice is limited. Carry enough food for two days in case of bad weather.

Drink

Water from the streams and lakes is generally safe to drink without treatment; take it from flowing water upstream of huts and campsites.

Stay safe

Weather changes fast, and snow is possible even in August. Tell the hut warden where you are going, and carry a map and compass as well as a phone. There is no mobile coverage on long stretches of the trail.

Do not try to ford rivers in spate; wait for the water to fall, usually by the morning.

Go next

  • Kiruna — the mining town and the Ice Hotel
  • Narvik — across the border in Norway
pages.wikivoyage/Dar_es_Salaam:
Dar es Salaam

Dar es Salaam

Dar es Salaam is the largest city in Tanzania and its commercial capital, a sprawling, humid port on the Indian Ocean with ferries to Zanzibar.

Understand

The name means "harbour of peace" in Arabic. The city grew from a fishing village after the Sultan of Zanzibar founded a palace here in 1865. Dodoma has been the official capital since 1996, but most government offices and embassies are still in Dar.

The hottest and most humid months are December to March. The long rains fall from March to May and flood many streets.

Get in

By plane

Julius Nyerere International Airport (DAR) is 12 km south-west of the city centre. A taxi to the centre costs TSh 40,000–50,000 and takes 45 minutes to two hours, depending on traffic. The BRT bus does not yet reach the airport.

By train

The new standard-gauge railway runs from the station near Kariakoo to Morogoro and Dodoma. The old TAZARA line runs twice a week to Kapiri Mposhi in Zambia, a journey of two to three days.

By boat

Fast ferries to Zanzibar leave from the terminal on Sokoine Drive four times a day and take about two hours. Buy tickets only at the company offices inside the terminal gate.

Get around

Traffic is notoriously bad. The Dar Rapid Transit (DART) buses run on their own lanes along Morogoro Road and Kawawa Road and are by far the quickest way across town; buy a card at the stations.

Bajajis (tuk-tuks) and boda-bodas are everywhere. Uber and Bolt are cheaper than street taxis.

See

The National Museum has the fossil skull of Paranthropus boisei found at Olduvai Gorge. Kariakoo Market is the city’s busiest market. The fish market at Kivukoni is busiest at dawn.

Do

Take a boat from the Slipway to Bongoyo Island for a beach day; the island is part of a marine reserve. Coco Beach on the Msasani peninsula is the city’s public beach and is crowded on Sundays.

Eat

Mishkaki (grilled meat skewers), chipsi mayai and fresh seafood are sold everywhere. Many restaurants on the Msasani peninsula cater to expatriates.

Sleep

Hotels in the city centre are convenient for the ferries; the Msasani peninsula has quieter, more expensive hotels. The Airport Lodge Hotel, five minutes from the terminal, has rooms from US$60 and a free airport shuttle.

Stay safe

Dar es Salaam has a reputation for street crime, and it is deserved in some areas. Bag snatching by thieves on motorbikes is common, so carry bags on the side away from the road and keep phones out of sight.

Muggings happen on Coco Beach, on the Selander Bridge and on the walk to the ferry terminal, especially after dark. Take a taxi at night even for short distances, and avoid deserted beaches at any time.

At the ferry terminal, touts sell fake tickets or offer to "help" with tickets for a fee; ignore them and go straight to the ticket offices. Never let anyone carry your luggage unless they are the ferry company’s own porters with badges.

Police roadblocks are common. Carry a copy of your passport and visa at all times, and keep calm and polite if stopped.

Do not photograph government buildings, the port, police or soldiers.

Stay healthy

Malaria and dengue fever are both present; dengue is spread by day-biting mosquitoes, so use repellent during the day too.

Tap water is not safe to drink; buy bottled water or boil it. Cholera outbreaks happen in the rainy season.

The Aga Khan Hospital on Ocean Road has a 24-hour emergency department and is the best equipped in the city. IST Clinic in Masaki has Western-trained doctors.

Connect

SIM cards are sold at the airport and in shops everywhere; registration needs a passport and a fingerprint scan.

Go next

  • Zanzibar — two hours by fast ferry
  • Bagamoyo — an old slave and ivory port, two hours north
pages.ifixit/Electric_Kettle_Heating_Element_R:
Electric Kettle Heating Element Replacement

Written By: Dana Okafor
  • Comments: 13

Difficulty

Moderate

Steps

8

Time Required

20 - 40 minutes

Introduction

Use this guide to replace the concealed heating element plate of a 1.7 litre cordless kettle that no longer heats.

Before you start, make sure the kettle is unplugged from its base and completely cool. Mains-voltage appliances can hold a charge in their capacitors; never test the kettle with the cover off while it is plugged in.

Tools

  • Phillips #1 Screwdriver

  • Tri-wing Y1 Screwdriver

  • Spudger

  • Multimeter

Parts

  • Kettle Heating Element Plate

  • Silicone Gasket

  1. Step 1

    • Unplug the base.

    • Empty the kettle and let it cool for at least 30 minutes.

    • Never open a kettle that is still connected to the mains or that contains water.

    I don't have a tri-wing driver. Can I use a small flathead?

    Mike - 3 March 2022

    A flathead will strip them. Buy the right bit, they are cheap.

    Replier - 4 March 2022

    Mine was the 2.2 litre model and the steps are the same.

    Ana - 3 March 2022

  2. Step 2

    • Turn the kettle upside down on a towel.

    • Remove the four 12 mm Phillips screws from the bottom cover.

    • Remove the two tri-wing screws hidden under the rubber feet.

    • Peel the feet off carefully with a spudger; they are held with adhesive and can be reused.

    On my kettle the hidden screws were under the label, not the feet.

    Kofi - 3 March 2022

    Thanks!

    Liz - 3 March 2022

    Three of mine were Phillips and one was tri-wing.

    Raj - 3 March 2022

    The screws are 10 mm on the newer model, not 12 mm.

    Bo - 3 March 2022

  3. Step 3

    • Lift off the bottom cover.

    • Photograph the wiring before you disconnect anything.

    • Pull the two spade connectors off the element terminals.

    • Pull on the connector, not the wire.

  4. Step 4

    • Use a multimeter on the resistance setting to measure across the element terminals.

    • A good 2,200 W element reads about 24 ohms.

    • A reading of zero or of infinity (open circuit) means the element has failed and must be replaced.

    Mine read 23.8 ohms and the kettle still didn't work. It was the thermostat in the end.

    Theo - 3 March 2022

  5. Step 5

    • Remove the three 8 mm Phillips screws holding the element plate.

    • Push the element plate up into the jug and lift it out with the old silicone gasket.

  6. Step 6

    • Fit the new silicone gasket around the new element plate.

    • Wet the gasket with a little water so that it slides into place.

    • Press the plate down evenly until the gasket is seated all the way round.

  7. Step 7

    • Refit the three 8 mm screws and tighten them in a criss-cross pattern so that the plate seats evenly.

    • Reconnect the spade connectors as in your photograph.

    • Refit the bottom cover and its screws.

  8. Step 8

Background and Identification

An electric kettle heats water with a resistive element of 1,800 to 3,000 watts, either a coil inside the jug or a flat plate under the floor. A bimetallic thermostat, usually a disc made by Strix or Otter, switches the kettle off when steam reaches it.

Troubleshooting

Kettle does not heat

  • Check that the base is plugged in and the socket works with another appliance.
  • The thermal fuse may have blown after the kettle was switched on empty. It is a small cylinder in the base, rated around 150 °C, and can be checked for continuity with a multimeter.
  • The element may have failed open circuit; measure its resistance.

Kettle does not switch off

If the kettle keeps boiling, the steam tube may be blocked by scale or the lid may not be closed. A worn thermostat disc can also fail to snap.

Maintenance

Descale the kettle every month in hard-water areas. Fill it half full with equal parts white vinegar and water, or with a solution of 2 tablespoons of citric acid per litre, bring it to the boil and leave it for an hour, then rinse well and boil fresh water twice.

Hand Crank Radio Troubleshooting

Common problems with emergency hand-crank and solar radios, and how to fix them.

Radio will not turn on

If the radio is dead whatever you do, work through these causes in order.

  • Flat battery
    • Crank the handle steadily for at least 3 minutes, about 2 turns a second; one minute of cranking gives roughly 15 minutes of radio
    • Leave the solar panel in direct sun for a full day if the battery has been flat for months
  • Worn-out rechargeable pack
    • Most of these radios use a 3.6 V NiMH pack or a single 18650 lithium cell; NiMH packs last about three years
    • Open the battery door on the back with a Phillips #1 screwdriver and check the pack for swelling or leaking
  • Broken crank gear
    • If the handle turns freely with no resistance, a tooth has broken off the plastic gear behind it

No sound but the light works

Check that the headphone socket is not stuck: a bent spring contact in the socket cuts off the speaker. Spraying contact cleaner into the socket and inserting and removing a plug a few times often fixes it.

Poor reception

  • Pull the telescopic antenna out fully for FM; for AM, turn the whole radio, because the AM antenna is a ferrite rod inside the case
  • Move away from LED lamps, phone chargers and solar inverters, which cause interference

Steps

5

Time Required

Introduction

Cup-and-cone hubs need their bearings cleaned and regreased about once a year, or sooner if they feel gritty. You will need cone spanners of the right size, usually 13 mm for front hubs and 15 mm for rear hubs.

Tools

  • 13 mm cone spanner

  • 15 mm cone spanner

  • Magnetic pickup tool

Parts

  • Bearing balls 3/16 inch

  • Waterproof grease

  1. Step 1

    • Remove the wheel from the bike. On a rear wheel, remove the cassette or freewheel first so that you can reach the drive-side cone.

  2. Step 2

    • Hold the cone with the cone spanner and undo the locknut on the non-drive side. Then unscrew the cone and slide the axle out of the hub.

    • Catch the balls as they fall: a front hub usually has ten 3/16 inch balls on each side, a rear hub nine 1/4 inch balls.

  3. Step 3

    • Clean the cups, cones and balls with degreaser and a rag. Look at the cones and cups closely under a light. Pitting or a dull track means the cone must be replaced.

  4. Step 4

    • Pack the cups with fresh waterproof grease and press the balls into the grease. The grease holds the balls in place while you refit the axle.

  5. Step 5

    • Screw the cone in until it just touches the balls, then back it off by about a quarter of a turn and tighten the locknut against it. The axle should turn smoothly with no play at the rim.

Refit the wheel and check that it spins freely.

Cookbook:Chapati

Chapati is an unleavened flatbread from the Indian subcontinent, also eaten throughout East Africa, where it is made with a little oil in the dough and fried on a flat pan.

CategoryBread recipes
Servings8 chapatis
Time1 hour
DifficultyEasy

Ingredients

  • 500 g (4 cups) wheat flour, plus extra for rolling
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 3 tablespoons vegetable oil, plus more for frying
  • 300 ml (1¼ cups) warm water

Procedure

  1. Make the dough:
    • Mix the flour and salt in a large bowl and make a well in the middle
    • Add the oil and most of the water and mix with your hand, adding the rest of the water a little at a time until a soft dough forms
    • Knead on a floured surface for about 10 minutes until smooth and elastic
  2. Cover the dough with a damp cloth and leave it to rest for 30 minutes; this makes the chapatis softer.
  3. Shape the chapatis:
    • Divide the dough into 8 balls
    • Roll each ball out into a thin circle about 20 cm across
    • Brush with oil, roll it up like a rope, coil the rope into a spiral and roll it flat again; this gives the flaky layers
  4. Cook:
    • Heat a heavy frying pan or tawa over medium-high heat without oil
    • Cook each chapati for about 1 minute until bubbles appear, turn it, brush with oil and cook for another minute until golden spots appear
    • Stack the cooked chapatis under a cloth to keep them soft

Notes, tips, and variations

  • Chapatis keep for two days wrapped in foil, and can be frozen
  • For a softer chapati, use warm milk instead of part of the water

Malaria

Malaria
SpecialtyInfectious disease
SymptomsFever, vomiting, headache, yellow skin
Usual onset10–15 days after exposure
CausesPlasmodium spread by mosquitoes
PreventionMosquito nets, insect repellent, mosquito control, medications
TreatmentAntimalarial medication
Deaths608,000 (2022)

Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease that affects humans and other vertebrates.[1] Symptoms usually begin ten to fifteen days after being bitten by an infected Anopheles mosquito.

Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites of the genus Plasmodium. It is spread by the bite of an infected female mosquito, which usually bites between dusk and dawn.

Signs and symptoms

  • Early symptoms
    • Fever, often coming in waves every two or three days, with shaking chills and then heavy sweating as the fever breaks
    • Headache, muscle and joint pains, tiredness and loss of appetite, which are easily mistaken for flu
    • Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, especially in children
  • Danger signs of severe malaria, which need hospital care at once
    • Confusion, drowsiness, fits or coma, signs that the brain is affected (cerebral malaria)
    • Difficulty breathing, or fast deep breathing caused by acid in the blood
    • Very dark or red urine, or passing little or no urine
    • Yellow eyes or skin, severe pallor from anaemia, or bleeding
    • In children, being unable to drink or breastfeed, or vomiting everything

Prevention

Methods used to prevent malaria include medications, mosquito elimination and the prevention of bites.[2]

  • Avoiding bites
    • Sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net every night, tucked in under the mattress, and check it for holes
    • Wear long sleeves and trousers after dusk and use repellent containing DEET, picaridin or IR3535 on exposed skin
    • Spray inside the house with insecticide and fit screens to windows and doors where possible
  • Mosquito control
    • Drain or cover standing water around the home, such as tyre tracks, buckets and blocked gutters, where mosquitoes breed
    • Indoor residual spraying of walls with long-lasting insecticides, carried out by health programmes
  • Medicines
    • Travellers should take preventive antimalarial tablets as advised by a doctor, starting before travel and continuing after return
    • In some areas, pregnant women and young children are given preventive treatment during the rainy season

Treatment

Malaria should be confirmed by a blood test or a rapid diagnostic test before treatment where possible. Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT); severe malaria is treated with injected artesunate in hospital.[3]

Epidemiology

In 2022 there were an estimated 249 million cases of malaria worldwide, causing about 608,000 deaths, most of them children under five in Africa.

pages.wikipedia/First_aid_kit:
First aid kit

A first aid kit is a collection of supplies and equipment used to give medical treatment.[1] There is a wide variation in the contents of first aid kits based on the knowledge and experience of those putting it together, the needs of the people who may use it, and where it will be used.

Kits are usually kept in a durable box or bag that is easy to carry, often marked with a white cross on a green background.

Contents

A basic kit for a home or a car should hold:[2]

  • For wounds
    • Sterile gauze pads and adhesive dressings (plasters) in several sizes
    • Roller bandages and a triangular bandage, which can also be used as a sling
    • Adhesive tape, scissors and tweezers for splinters
  • For protection
    • Disposable gloves, so that blood does not touch your skin
    • A face shield or pocket mask for giving rescue breaths
  • Other items
    • A thermometer, safety pins and a foil blanket to keep an injured person warm
    • Saline solution or clean water in sealed pods to wash wounds and eyes
    • A first aid manual and a list of emergency telephone numbers

Containers

Commercial kits are made of hard plastic or of fabric pouches. Kits for wet places, such as boats, are made with waterproof seals. Wall-mounted cabinets made of metal are used in workplaces.

In many countries, the law says what a workplace kit must hold; these lists are made with the number of workers and the hazards of the work in mind.

Maintenance

Kits should be checked every few months. Items used should be replaced, and medicines and sterile items past their expiry date thrown away.

pages.wikipedia/Milk:
Milk

Milk is a white liquid food produced by the mammary glands of mammals.[1] It is the main source of nutrition for young mammals before they are able to digest solid food.

Cow’s milk is about 87% water, 4.6% lactose (milk sugar), 3.7% fat, 3.3% protein and 0.7% minerals. It contains calcium, phosphorus, vitamin B12 and vitamin A.[2]

Production

In 2021 the world produced about 918 million tonnes of milk, most of it from cows. Large amounts of milk also come from buffalo in India and Pakistan, and from goats, sheep and camels.

Processing

Most milk is pasteurised, by heating it to 72 °C for 15 seconds, to kill harmful bacteria. Homogenisation breaks up the fat globules so that cream does not rise to the top.

Products

Butter is made from cream churned until the fat separates. Cheese is made from milk curdled with rennet or acid. Yoghurt is made with bacteria that turn lactose into lactic acid. Skimmed milk powder is made by evaporating the water from skimmed milk.

Infant formula is usually made from cow’s milk with its proteins and fats changed to resemble human milk more closely. Condensed milk is mixed with sugar.

Lactose intolerance

Most adults in the world produce less lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose, after weaning. Drinking milk can then cause bloating, wind and diarrhoea. Yoghurt and hard cheese contain little lactose and are often tolerated.

Human milk

Human milk has more lactose and less protein than cow’s milk. The World Health Organization recommends breastfeeding alone for the first six months of life.

pages.wikipedia/Obsidian:
Obsidian

Obsidian is a naturally occurring volcanic glass formed when lava extruded from a volcano cools rapidly with minimal crystal growth.[1] It is an igneous rock.

Obsidian is mineral-like, but not a true mineral because, as a glass, it is not crystalline. It is about 70% or more silica (silicon dioxide), with oxides of aluminium, sodium and potassium; small amounts of iron and magnesium give it its dark colour.

Occurrence

Obsidian is found near volcanoes in places that have had rhyolitic eruptions, for example in Armenia, Turkey, Italy, Mexico, Kenya and the western United States.

Use by people

Because it breaks with very sharp, smooth curved edges, obsidian was valued in the Stone Age for cutting tools. Knife blades, arrowheads and spear points were knapped from it, and it was traded hundreds of kilometres from its sources.[2]

The Aztecs and Maya made mirrors and the edges of the macuahuitl, a wooden club, from it. Obsidian blades are still sometimes used as surgical scalpels, as their edge is many times thinner than that of a steel blade.

Dating

Obsidian slowly absorbs water at its surface. Measuring the thickness of this hydration rind is a way of dating obsidian tools.

pages.wikivoyage/Kisumu:
Kisumu

Kisumu

Kisumu is Kenya’s third city, a relaxed port on the shore of Lake Victoria and the gateway to western Kenya.

Understand

The city is hot and humid, at 1,130 m above sea level. Dholuo, Swahili and English are spoken.

Get in

By plane

  • Kisumu International Airport (KIS), 3 km west of the centre. Several flights a day from Nairobi, taking 50 minutes.
    • A taxi to the centre costs about KSh 800 and takes 15 minutes
    • Matatus to the centre stop on the main road outside the airport gate and cost KSh 50
    • Boda-bodas wait at the arrivals hall and cost about KSh 200 to town

By train

The restored metre-gauge line from Nakuru brings a weekly train, the Kisumu Safari Train, arriving on Saturday afternoon.

By bus

Buses from Nairobi take about seven hours. Easy Coach and Guardian Angel are the most reliable companies.

Get around

The centre is compact and walkable. Tuk-tuks and boda-bodas go everywhere for KSh 50–200.

See

Kisumu Impala Sanctuary, on the lake shore, has impala, zebra and a walking trail. Dunga Beach is a fishing village where boats can be hired to see hippos.

Do

Take a boat trip on the lake at sunset from Dunga Beach for about KSh 2,000 per boat.

Eat

Fried tilapia from the lake with ugali is the local dish; the fish restaurants on Dunga Beach and along the shore serve it.

Sleep

Hotels in the centre range from basic lodgings to the Acacia Premier, a business hotel with a rooftop pool.

Stay safe

Do not swim in the lake: bilharzia (schistosomiasis) is common and hippos and crocodiles are present.

Stay healthy

Malaria is a risk all year. Use a net and repellent.

Go next

  • Kakamega Forest — the last tropical rainforest in Kenya, two hours north

The year 1903 in science and technology involved some significant events, listed below.[1]

Events

  • January
    • January 19 – The first transatlantic radio broadcast from the United States to Britain is sent from a station on Cape Cod, a greeting from President Roosevelt to King Edward VII

    • December 17 – Orville and Wilbur Wright make the first controlled, sustained flights of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, the longest lasting 59 seconds and covering 852 feet
    • December 22 – The Royal Society in London hears a report from a commission sent to Uganda that sleeping sickness is carried by the tsetse fly
    • December 30 – Fire at the Iroquois Theater in Chicago kills more than 600 people and leads to new rules on fire exits and asbestos safety curtains in theatres

Births

  • April 17 – Nicholas Rescher, mathematician (died 1999)

Burn

Burn
SpecialtyDermatology, plastic surgery
SymptomsSuperficial: red without blisters; partial thickness: blisters and pain; full thickness: area stiff and not painful
ComplicationsInfection
DurationDays to weeks
TypesSuperficial, partial thickness, full thickness
CausesHeat, cold, electricity, chemicals, friction, radiation
TreatmentDepends on severity
Frequency67 million (2015)

A burn is an injury to skin, or other tissues, caused by heat, cold, electricity, chemicals, friction or ultraviolet radiation.[1] Most burns are due to heat from hot liquids (called scalding), solids or fire.

Burns that affect only the outer skin layer (superficial burns) are red without blisters and heal in about a week; partial-thickness burns blister and are painful; full-thickness burns may be white, leathery or charred and painless.

First aid

  • Cool the burn
    • Hold the burnt area under cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible and within three hours of the injury
    • Remove rings, watches and clothing near the burn unless they are stuck to the skin
  • Cover the burn
    • Lay cling film or a clean plastic bag loosely over the burn, which keeps it clean and eases the pain
  • Do not
    • Do not apply butter, oil, toothpaste, egg white or other home remedies, which trap heat and can cause infection
    • Do not use ice or iced water, which can damage the skin further and cause hypothermia, especially in children
    • Do not burst blisters or peel away loose skin

Get medical help for burns larger than the person’s hand, for burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals or across joints, for chemical and electrical burns, and for any burn in a baby or a young child.[2]

Treatment

In hospital, burns are cleaned and dressed. Large burns need intravenous fluids, calculated from the weight of the person and the area burnt. Deep burns may need skin grafts.

Prevention

Turn pan handles inward on the stove, set water heaters no higher than 50 °C, keep hot drinks away from small children, and fit smoke alarms.

Beekeeping/Installing a package

A package of bees is a screened box holding about 1.4 kg of worker bees and a caged queen, sold in spring to start a new colony.

Before you begin

Have the hive set up on its stand before the bees arrive, with frames of foundation and a feeder of sugar syrup made of one part sugar to one part water by weight.

Step 1

Spray the bees through the screen with a little sugar syrup. This calms them and gives them something to do. Do not soak them.

Step 2

Remove the feeder can and the queen cage from the package. Check that the queen is alive and keep her cage in the shade.

Step 3

Remove the cork from the candy end of the queen cage and hang the cage between two middle frames, candy end up. The workers will eat through the candy and release her in two or three days.

Step 4

Shake the bees into the hive over the frames with a firm downward jerk. Replace the frames gently and close the hive.

After installation

Do not open the hive for a week, except to refill the feeder. After seven days check that the queen has been released and is laying eggs.

Wilderness first aid/Splints

A splint holds a broken or badly sprained limb still, to ease pain and prevent further injury while the person is moved to help.

Kinds of splint

  1. Rigid splints

    Rigid splints are made from boards, sticks, rolled magazines or a folded foam sleeping mat, padded and tied above and below the injury.
    • Pad the hollows, such as behind the knee, with clothing so that the splint does not press on the skin
    • Tie it firmly but check the fingers or toes every 15 minutes for colour, warmth and feeling

  2. Soft splints

    A pillow or rolled blanket wrapped round a forearm or ankle and tied in place makes a soft splint.

  3. Anatomical splints

    An injured leg can be tied to the good leg with padding between them, and a finger to the next finger with tape.

When not to move a limb

Do not try to straighten a limb that is badly bent at a joint, or any limb with bone showing; splint it in the position found.
